desc:
The array nums holds colours numbered 1 to k. Sort the array in non-decreasing order of colour and return it.

nums = [3, 2, 2, 1, 4], k = 4
result = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]

Do it without a comparison sort and without counting every colour into a table of size k: the intended solution partitions the array in place and runs in O(n log k) time with O(1) extra space (apart from the recursion/stack). It generalises the three-colour Dutch flag problem.
hints: With k = 2 this is a single partition: move the 1s to the left and the 2s to the right with two pointers.
For larger k, split the colour range in halves. Partition the array so that colours in the lower half come first, then repeat on each part with the half range.

Recurse (or use an explicit stack) on triples (left, right, lowColor, highColor). Take mid = (lowColor + highColor) // 2, partition nums[left..right] so that colours ≤ mid are on the left, then process the two sides with ranges [lowColor, mid] and [mid + 1, highColor]. Stop when the segment is empty or the colour range has one value.
editorial: This is a recursive version of quicksort's partition where the pivot is a colour boundary instead of an element. Splitting the colour range at its midpoint guarantees a depth of about log<sub>2</sub> k, and at every level each element is touched once by a partition step, so the total work is O(n log k).

A two-pointer partition for the range [l, r]: i moves right while nums[i] ≤ mid, j moves left while nums[j] > mid, and if i < j the two elements are swapped. When the pointers cross, [l, j] holds the low colours and [i, r] the high colours.

Counting the occurrences of each colour in an array of size k is also O(n + k) and perfectly fine in practice; the partition approach shines when k is large and memory is tight, or when the elements are heavy records that you do not want to copy.
